clinicalPearls: Heterotopic ossification is the formation of mature lamellar bone within soft tissues where bone does not normally exist, most often around large joints
It is common after spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, major joint surgery, burns, and severe trauma, typically appearing within weeks to a few months of the inciting event
Early presentation can mimic infection or thrombosis, with localised swelling, warmth, erythema, pain, and progressive loss of joint range of motion
A markedly raised serum alkaline phosphatase supports early disease but is non-specific and can be normal, so imaging is important
Plain radiographs are often normal early; triple-phase bone scan is the most sensitive method for detecting immature heterotopic bone before it is visible on x-ray
Maintaining joint range of motion through careful therapy is central to management, alongside prophylaxis in high-risk patients using measures such as NSAIDs and, in selected cases, radiation
Bisphosphonates may be used to limit mineralisation of immature lesions as part of medical management
Surgical excision is reserved for mature, well-established lesions that significantly limit function, ideally once bone activity has settled to reduce recurrence risk
The most disabling consequence is ankylosis of a joint, which can severely impair positioning, mobility, and self-care
reference.pathophysiology: Heterotopic ossification involves aberrant differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts within soft tissue, driven by a combination of an osteogenic local environment, tissue injury and inflammation, and neurogenic signalling in patients with central nervous system injury. Inflammatory mediators and bone morphogenetic proteins promote the formation of an osteoid matrix that subsequently mineralises into mature bone. The process evolves from an early inflammatory and immature phase through progressive mineralisation to eventual mature lamellar bone.
additionalInvestigations: Serial serum alkaline phosphatase to support diagnosis and monitor activity
Triple-phase bone scintigraphy for early and sensitive detection of immature lesions
Plain radiographs to characterise and follow established, mineralised bone
Ultrasound or CT for further definition and surgical planning
Doppler ultrasound and inflammatory markers to exclude thrombosis and infection
redFlags: Presentation mimicking deep vein thrombosis or septic arthritis that must be excluded urgently
Rapidly progressive joint ankylosis threatening irreversible loss of function
Ossification compressing a peripheral nerve or vessel
Skin breakdown or pressure injury developing over a fixed, ossified joint
reference.prognosis: Many lesions stabilise without causing major functional loss, but a significant proportion progress to restrict joint movement, and severe cases cause complete ankylosis. Outcomes are improved by early recognition, preserving range of motion, and appropriately timed prophylaxis or surgery.
pitfalls: Attributing early swelling and warmth solely to thrombosis or infection and missing the diagnosis
Relying on early plain radiographs, which are frequently negative in immature disease
Aggressive forced manipulation of the affected joint, which may aggravate the lesion
Operating on immature, metabolically active bone, increasing the risk of recurrence
Neglecting prophylaxis in high-risk patients such as those with spinal cord or brain injury
management: Offer prophylaxis in high-risk patients using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as indometacin and, in selected cases, low-dose radiotherapy to suppress aberrant osteogenesis
Preserve joint range of motion through careful physiotherapy and gentle mobilisation, the central aim of management
Consider bisphosphonate therapy to slow mineralisation of immature lesions in selected cases

Reserve surgical excision for established mature bone causing functional impairment, timed once activity has settled on bone scan and alkaline phosphatase, with peri-operative prophylaxis to reduce recurrence
Provide analgesia and treat the local inflammatory phase symptomatically
Exclude mimics of the early presentation such as deep vein thrombosis and infection before attributing swelling to heterotopic bone
Coordinate rehabilitation-led multidisciplinary care to optimise function and time interventions
